newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown raises taxes to cool economy.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown raises taxes to cool economy.

text.p: Finance minister Gordon Brown raised taxes on Wednesday to slow Britain's surging economy in a maiden budget that pumped more money into schools and hospitals and gave firms incentives to boost investment.

Unveiling what he called "a people's budget", the first by a Labour government in 18 years, Brown also redeemed his party's main election pledge by slapping a net 4.8 billion pound ($8 billion) "windfall" tax on the excess profits of utilities that Labour believes were privatised too cheaply by the previous Conservative government.
The money will finance a 3.5 billion pound welfare-to-work programme, to create what Brown called a "ladder of opportunity" for Britain's army of young and long-term unemployed.
"Previous budgets pursued the short-term interests of the few. This budget advances the long-term interests of the many.
"A budget equipping Britain for the future -- meeting the people's priorities," Brown told a packed House of Commons (lower house).

The wide-ranging budget contained a host of measures that will mean higher taxes for homeowners and car drivers, slash the income of pension funds and help meet the government's ambitious environmental goals.

With rapid consumer spending risking an unsustainable boom, Brown said he would raise an extra 5.5 billion pounds ($9.1 billion) in tax this year and 4.75 billion pounds next year to put Britain on the road to long-term financial stability.
"I will not ignore the warning signs and I will not repeat past mistakes," Brown, said. "This and future budgets will be addressed to laying the foundations for tomorrow's wealth."
Under the government's plans, its budget deficit will fall sharply to just 4.0 billion pounds, or 0.25 percent of national income, in the 1998-1999 budget year.
But, economists doubted that Brown had raised taxes by enough to persuade the newly independent Bank of England, worried about inflationary pressures, to hold off from raising interest rates.
Brown surprised members of parliament by proposing a series of measures to remedy Britain's poor investment record, which he said had lagged that of its main competitors since 1980.
"The central purpose of this budget is to ensure that Britain is equipped to rise to the challenge of the new and fast-changing global economy," he said.

He cut the main rate of tax on company profits from 33 percent to a record low of 31 percent and, arguing that small businesses in future will be the main engine of job creation, trimmed their tax rate to 21 percent from 23 percent.

In a further step to encourage firms to plough more profits back into investment instead of paying them out in dividends, Brown also abolished tax credits paid to pension funds -- estimated to be worth more than three billion pounds.
William Hague, the new leader of the main opposition Conservative Party, attacked the tax credit move and the windfall tax as a "double whammy" for pension funds.
"The bills for the decisions announced today will be paid by millions of hard-working people many years down the line.
"It is a smash and grab raid on pensions funds in this country and it is a cynical betrayal of the millions who have built up pensions and now see them devalued," Hague said.

Labour supporters were cheered by Brown's unexpected announcement that he would dig into the Treasury's contingency reserves to provide an extra 1.2 billion pounds for the cash-strapped health service and one billion pounds for schools.
In addition, he said, the windfall tax would fund a 1.3 billion pound programme over five years to repair crumbling classrooms and provide computers and other equipment.
"If our schools are to educate for the needs of the 21st century economy, they must themselves become schools fit to learn in and equipped for the 21st century," he said.

He also acted to take steam out of Britain's bubbling housing market by trimming the tax break homeowners get on mortgage interest payments and by increasing tax payable on purchases of expensive homes.
The budget speech was delayed by about 20 minutes as MPs debated a Conservative accusation that some details of the budget had been leaked to newspapers on Tuesday night.
($ = 0.602 British Pounds)
